title: A nonsolvable group with a central torus of codimension three is reductive
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $H$ be a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A torus is a closed subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$, with $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$; maximal means maximal among these subgroups. A smooth affine group is unipotent if all its geometric points in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation satisfy $(u-I)^n=0$ for some $n\geq1$. Reductive means having no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Let $Z\subseteq H$ be a central torus, where central means that every section of $Z$ commutes with every section of $H$ after every commutative $k$-algebra extension. Write $\dim$ for topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Suppose $\dim H=\dim Z+3$ and $H$ is not solvable; solvable means that its scheme-theoretic derived series, formed by the closed subgroup generated by each commutator morphism, terminates at the identity. Then $H$ is reductive. No condition on the rank of $Z$ or on the characteristic of $k$ is imposed.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/luminysga3smf.pdf . Proposition 3.1.9 proof (1), printed p.88, paragraph beginning with the central torus: nonsolvable three-dimensional quotient and the dimension-at-most-two solvability argument. Field lemma isolating that argument, not a relative openness assertion.

proof.text: Centrality makes $Z$ normal. Form the affine fppf quotient $q:H\to Q=H/Z$ using [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Its kernel is $Z$, and $q$ is faithfully flat and finitely presented; $Q$ is smooth and connected. Over the algebraically closed field, geometric connectedness is supplied by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. The dimension formula [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image], applied to the factorization $H\to Q\xrightarrow{1}Q$, gives $\dim H=\dim Q+\dim Z$, hence $\dim Q=3$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(1), proof, printed p.88, central-torus quotient; expanded by Milne Theorem 5.28, Propositions 5.23, 5.29 and Remark 5.42.

proof.text: The group $Q$ is not solvable. Otherwise choose $b$ with $D^bQ=1$. The derived subgroups of $H$ and $Q$ exist and remain smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]; each $D^{j+1}Q$ is normal in $D^jQ$. We show by induction that $q$ maps $D^jH$ into $D^jQ$; the case $j=0$ is clear. If $q(D^jH)\subseteq D^jQ$, form the quotient $D^jQ\to D^jQ/D^{j+1}Q$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]; its kernel is $D^{j+1}Q$, and it is commutative because the commutator morphism of $D^jQ$ factors through $D^{j+1}Q$ and $D^jQ\to D^jQ/D^{j+1}Q$ is an fppf epimorphism. The composite $D^jH\to D^jQ\to D^jQ/D^{j+1}Q$ is a homomorphism to a commutative affine group, hence trivial on $D^{j+1}H$ by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]; so $q$ maps $D^{j+1}H$ into the kernel $D^{j+1}Q$. Thus $D^bH\subseteq\ker q=Z$. Since a torus is commutative, the commutator morphism of $D^bH$ is trivial and $D^{b+1}H=1$, contradicting the hypothesis on $H$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(1), proof, printed p.88: nonsolvability of the three-dimensional quotient; elementary derived-series expansion, with Milne Section 6(d)-(e).

proof.text: Let $N\subseteq H$ be any nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Both $N$ and $Q$ are separated by [lem-sc-group-scheme-separated-field]. Factor $q|_N$ as $N\twoheadrightarrow I\hookrightarrow Q$ by [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization]. Since $I$ is closed in the affine $Q$, it is affine, and the flat surjective $N\to I$ is faithfully flat on coordinate algebras (a flat ring map whose Spec map is surjective is faithfully flat), as the next lemma requires. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-normal-quotient-image] to $q:H\to Q$ and $N$: $I$ is smooth, connected, normal and unipotent. If $I=1$, then $N\hookrightarrow H$ factors through $\ker q=Z$. By [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] this homomorphism $N\to Z$ is trivial; since its composite into $H$ is the subgroup inclusion, $N=1$, a contradiction. Hence $I\ne1$. Applying the strict dimension inequality of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] to $1\subsetneq I$ gives $\dim I\geq1$.

source.place: Theorem 5.39; Corollary 14.7; Corollary 14.18(a); the dimension argument of Proposition 6.42. These expand the unipotent-radical argument in Conrad Proposition 3.1.9(1), p.88.

proof.text: Form $p:Q\to R=Q/I$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Again $R$ is smooth, connected, affine and of finite type. The dimension formula [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image] gives $3=\dim Q=\dim R+\dim I$. Consequently $0\leq\dim R\leq2$, so [lem-sfb-connected-group-dimension-two-solvable] shows that $R$ is solvable.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(1), proof, printed p.88, dimension-at-most-two quotient; Milne Corollary 17.27, printed p.360.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable], $I$ has a finite series with commutative successive quotients. Pull back the derived series $R=D^0R\supseteq\cdots\supseteq D^bR=1$ along $p$ and append that series for $I=\ker p$. The correspondence and quotient assertions of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identify each quotient in the pulled-back series with $D^jR/D^{j+1}R$, which is commutative by the definition of the derived subgroup. Existence of all the derived terms follows from [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]. Thus we obtain a finite series $Q=Q_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq Q_c=1$ with $[Q_j,Q_j]\subseteq Q_{j+1}$. By induction and the minimality defining the derived subgroup, $D^jQ\subseteq Q_j$ for every $j$. Therefore $D^cQ=1$, contradicting step 2.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, printed pp.284-285; Proposition 6.27 and Proposition 6.30, printed pp.131-132. The elementary pullback-and-concatenation argument is written out.

proof.text: No nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup $N$ of $H$ can therefore exist. Together with the given smoothness, connectedness and affineness, this is exactly reductivity as defined in the statement.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(1), proof, printed p.88, conclusion of the central-torus argument.
